h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to judge which settings are strong, weak or neutral, and which parts other settings can cut off from the outcome. Build hypotheses mainly from (a) the edited field's current parent value: replacing a strong value with a weak one hurts, and filling an empty or harmful slot helps; and (b) conditions that disconnect the edited part, pushing its effect toward zero. Directions refer to the signed effect, not its size. Disconnection makes the effect lower only if the edit usually helps, and higher if it usually hurts. If the usual sign is unclear, do not use it. When finding flaws, check this sign logic first. Replace any hypothesis whose direction could reverse through a competing effect or that relies on partial redundancy. Vary edit fields and values. State a one-sentence mechanism.

hyps.why: With edge 0 removed node 1 is zero, so a conv on edge 4 carries nothing and its usual gain vanishes.
Edge 2 reads from node 1, which is dead when edge 0 is none, so the edit has no effect.
A conv on edge 4 normally helps but carries nothing when node 1 is cut off from the input.
Edge 2 is fed only through node 1, so with edge 0 absent the added conv has no input.
Adding a conv to an empty direct edge gives a larger gain than upgrading an edge that already carries an op.
Restoring the edge from node 2 to the output with a strong conv helps more than swapping one active op for another.
Filling an empty edge with the strongest op gives the largest gain, while upgrading an existing op gives less.
Removing a strong conv on the edge feeding node 1 hurts, while removing an already-absent or weak op costs little.
Deleting a strong conv into the output loses more than deleting a weak op.
Adding a conv to the empty direct input-to-output edge gains more than changing an op that is already there.
